judge.rationale: Integrity holds: no clipped or placeholder content across all ten pages; slide 10's numbered list does show a formatting slip where item 1 wraps oddly ("per slide 8." orphaned) and items 2-4 lose their numbers, rendering as plain paragraphs while item 1 is numbered — a real but minor inconsistency rather than a break. Legibility is fine at board scale: dark blue titles on white, orange/blue chart series that are distinguishable, table headers in blue bands. Coherence is strong and clearly systematic: every page carries a small caps orange eyebrow (EXECUTIVE SUMMARY, THE MEASUREMENT, CURRENT STATE), the same blue title, the same footer rule with "Capital Allocation Review" left and page number right; the callout card treatment repeats consistently (11.8% on p5, 14.3% on p6, +2.5 pts and EUR 0 on p9, the annotation boxes for Division C/D on p4). Communicatively it is genuinely good: titles are conclusions not labels ("Returns diverge sharply by division; capital does not follow them", "Allocation has tracked revenue share, not return", "Blended portfolio return builds from 11.8% to 14.3% over the plan"), the p3 bar chart is annotated with per-division callouts naming highest/second/largest-user/lowest, p5 vs p6 is a well-judged before/after of the same EUR 120m, p8 gives an explicit year-by-year glide path with a footnote, and units are consistent (EUR m, %, pts). The weakest analytic page is p4, where the paired revenue-share/incremental-return columns are unlabelled on the y-axis (a single 0-40% scale mixing share of capital and return is ambiguous) and the two annotation boxes float in the plot's whitespace rather than sitting on a grid. Sourcing is thin — footnotes appear only on p8; the charts on p3, p4 and p9 have no source line. Craft is above template level: the p1 title slide with three stat cards, the deliberate p5/p6 mirror, and the p9 line chart paired with two stacked result cards read as composed for this argument. It stops short of level 5 on the p10 list numbering defect, the missing chart sources, and p4's axis ambiguity. Genericness is low-mid: the structure and the same-money-reweighted device are specific to this brief, but the blue/orange-on-white palette and card motifs are standard consulting furniture that would transfer unchanged to any other deck.

Integrity holds: no clipped text, no placeholder strings, every one of the ten slides is populated. Legibility is the first real strain — slide 4's three option cards set their body copy ('Selective price match, only where a specific account is at risk of losing') at a size that is visibly smaller than any other body text in the deck, and slide 8's comparison table pushes row labels and the footnote below it into the same too-small band; slide 3's chart axis labels and the legend ('Our price / Competitor price / Competitor breakeven floor') are near-illegible at deck scale. Those are borderline rather than fatal, so the deck clears level 2 but stops at 3 for coherence reasons and never reaches 4.

Visual coherence is the deck's strength and also where it caps out: consistent blue eyebrow + blue headline + rule, consistent 'What this buys us / What it costs us' two-column body on slides 5, 6 and 7, and a repeated blue metric strip at the foot of each option slide. But the repetition is mechanical rather than composed — slides 5, 6 and 7 are the same slide three times with swapped words, and slide 4's card treatment (accent bars in blue/orange/green) introduces a colour system that never appears again, so the option colour-coding does not carry through to the option slides or to the table on slide 8. Slide 3's callout box 'The 8-point gap' sits in a plain grey panel that matches nothing else in the deck.

Communicative effectiveness fails the level-4 bar in specific places. Slide 3's chart has no stated units on the y-axis beyond 'Price index' and no source line under it, while slide 2 does carry a source; that inconsistency is exactly what level 4 forbids. The blue metric strips on 5/6/7 compress four numbers into a single line ('Year 1 revenue: -1% | Year 1 margin: -4.5 pts | Time to impact: 2-4 weeks | Investment: Low') with no visual differentiation between the numbers and the labels, so the reader cannot compare across options without holding three slides in memory — and slide 8, the table that should resolve that, uses red/green colouring on only some cells with no key. Slide 9's recommendation is four bullets of running prose on a blue field rather than a decision-shaped page; for the one slide the executive team will act on, it does the least work.

Craft: the composition reads as a competent consulting template with the brief's content poured in. The blue-and-white palette, the eyebrow-plus-headline pattern, and the two-column pro/con body would be identical for a pricing deck, a market-entry deck or a reorg deck. Nothing in the visual language is specific to a price-attack narrative — the one chance to make the argument visual, the breakeven-floor chart on slide 3, is a default three-bar chart rather than a designed exhibit.

I would not send this unchanged: the missing source and units on slide 3, the sub-legible card copy on slide 4, and the unexplained red/green in the slide 8 table would each draw a question in the room.

Integrity holds: no clipping, overlap or placeholder text on any of the 11 pages, and every table (6, 8, 10) and chart (3, 5) is fully populated. Legibility is adequate, though the workstream table on 6 and the cadence table on 8 push toward the smallest type in the deck and would be marginal for the back of a room of twenty. Coherence is largely there — consistent eyebrow labels ('WHY NOW', 'THE TARGET', 'GOVERNANCE'), blue title rule, and footer/page-number treatment across 2-11. Where it slips: the three cards on page 4 carry text only in the top third and leave roughly half of each card empty, so the row reads as unfinished rather than airy; and colour is used decoratively rather than semantically — the five bars on page 5 are blue/orange/green/yellow with no encoded meaning, while the same palette on 7 and 9 does carry meaning (steering vs PMO vs workstream; mobilise/design/launch). Level 4 is not met: neither the margin line chart on 3 nor the savings bar chart on 5 carries a source line, and the workstream split is restated three times — as bars on 5, as a table with target/share/lever on 6, and again as targets in the accountability table on 10 — so a twelve-slide deck spends three slides on one fact. The '-6 pts' callout on 3 and the '€40M' anchor on 5 are the two moments that do earn their space. Titles are conclusion-shaped throughout ('Margin down 6 points in two years — while peers held', 'The rhythm that keeps €40M on track'), and units and dates are present in the owner table on 10, which is the deck's strongest page. Visually it is a competent blue-and-orange consulting shell: swap the €40M for any other number and the same eleven layouts would serve unchanged.

Integrity holds — no clipping, no placeholder text, all 11 pages populated — and type is legible with black-on-white contrast throughout, so levels 1 and 2 pass. Level 3 fails on several counts. The two charts are unstyled defaults in a deck that is otherwise pure black/white/grey: page 4's bar chart carries a colour legend ('Promised'/'Actual') for two bars, a y-axis running 0–5 with unlabelled 'Weeks' semantics, and grey/black bars that appear nowhere else in the system; page 8's chart is a single black bar plus a stub bar with a two-item legend ('Believed by sales'/'Actual (survey)') that duplicates what the two bars already say, and its y-axis label '% of lost-deal reasons' is rotated and tiny. Neither chart matches the flat grey-block treatment used for the stat cards on pages 2, 6 and 8. Rhythm also breaks: pages 5, 7, 9 and 11 are title-plus-bullet-list slides with an enormous empty lower half — page 11 in particular has four bullets and roughly 60% dead space with a stray italic 'Questions and discussion welcome' floating at the bottom. Pages 4, 6 and 8 all use the same left-visual/right-stat-block split but with different visual widths and different vertical alignment of the right column. Level 4 also fails independently: neither chart states a source or a takeaway inside the chart, page 4's y-axis has no unit on the scale, and the '+125%' and '40% vs 11%' figures sit as raw numerals with caption text below rather than as titled callouts. Titles do carry conclusions ('Pricing is not the objection sales believes it is', 'The reporting module is the reason customers renew'), which is the deck's strongest quality. Genericness is high: aside from the numbers, this is a stock black-and-white eyebrow/title/body wireframe — the three-card row on page 3, the black-header table on page 10 and the bullet slides would be identical for any research readout in any industry.

Integrity holds across all 15 pages: no clipped text, no empty frames, no lorem — the KPI tiles on p2 (EUR 23m / EUR 4.2m/yr / EUR 6.1m/yr / 3 of 5), the gate table on p12 and the risk tables on p13-14 all render complete rows, and the p11 phase bar sits clear of the three phase cards. Legibility is adequate but is the weakest rung: the risk-table body copy on p13 and especially the 'How we manage it' column on p14 is set very small for a projected committee deck, and the right-hand assumption block on p5 and the axis-note on p9 ('Illustrative annual phasing...') sit near the floor of readable size. Coherence is genuinely strong — the eyebrow/title/footer triple repeats identically on every page, the black title slide (p1) is the only inversion, charts on p4, p5, p9, p10 share one axis, tick and label treatment, and the boxed-panel motif on p3, p6 and p15 is the same box. Communicatively it does the job an IC deck must: titles conclude rather than label ('Doing nothing still costs EUR 25m over six years — and that is the conservative number', p5; 'Cumulative value turns positive in year six, then compounds', p10; 'Replace is the only option that meets every criterion', p8), the alternatives matrix on p7 ends in an explicit Recommended row, and units are carried on the numbers. What stops it at 4 rather than 5 is compositional slack and chart plainness: p6 leaves roughly the bottom third empty under four short boxes, p8's six ticks float in a half-empty page, p15's ask is three bullets plus three tiles with a large dead band between, and the charts on p4 and p5 are unadorned default bars/lines — no highlighted final point, no callout on the crossover year that p10's title claims. On genericness, the content is unmistakably this brief (retirement clock, gate releases, EUR 23m/6.1m), but the visual language — pure monochrome, thin rules, boxed KPI tiles — is the neutral consulting default and would transfer unchanged to any other investment case.

Integrity holds: no clipped text, no placeholder strings, no overlap. The three lever slides (7, 8, 9) repeat a disciplined pattern — big percentage, euro contribution, two pill chips for confidence/investment, three bullets — and the lever colour coding (expansion green, adjacent orange, pricing blue-violet) is honoured on the summary table (2), the bridge (5), the split table (6), the phasing bars (11), the risk table (12) and the approval cards (13). Titles are conclusions, not labels: 'Expansion is the largest, safest lever: EUR 38m from a 22% attach rate' (7), 'Pricing adds EUR 23m fast — but it's the most fragile lever' (9). Units are attached to every figure and slide 5 carries a rounding note. That clears levels 1-3 and most of 4. What keeps it off 5 is craft detail rather than error. Slide 10's 2x2 is the weakest artefact: the quadrant labels ('Quick wins', 'Moonshots', 'Best-in-class'?) and both axis captions sit at a size that will not survive a printed board pack, the bubble areas encode nothing the reader is told, and the three bubbles cluster left of centre leaving the right half of the plot empty. Slides 3 and 4 spend their bottom third on nothing after a single sentence, so the big-number treatment reads generous on 3 and thin on 4. Table widths disagree: the exec-summary table (2) runs to the full text column, while the risk table (12) and checkpoint table (14) stop short of the right margin, so the grid does not repeat cleanly. Chart takeaways are also uneven — 11 gets a cumulative-revenue caption under the bars, but 5's bridge relies on the label strip beneath it and carries no source line. Sendable to a board with a light pass on slide 10's type sizes and the two narrow tables. On genericness: the content is unmistakably this brief — attach rate, three levers, confidence/investment pairs, FY27-FY29 checkpoints — but the visual language (navy cover, small-caps eyebrow, thin rules, footer confidentiality line, green/orange/blue accents) is the default consulting readout and would look identical for a cost-reduction or M&A deck with the numbers swapped.

Integrity holds: no clipped text, no placeholder strings, no overlap I can see across all twelve pages; the bar chart on page 4, the bubble matrix on page 6 and the reallocation table on page 10 all render fully with labels and footnotes. Legibility is adequate at deck scale, with the weakest points being the sub-caption under the stat row on page 3 and the footnote/row type in the page 10 table, both of which sit near the floor for projection. Coherence is genuinely good: the eyebrow-plus-assertion title lockup repeats on every page, the footer and page numbers are consistent, and pages 7-9 form a deliberate triptych — big numeral, colour-coded rule (red/green/blue), matching bullet column, full-width action bar. The arithmetic is internally consistent (11+4+8=23 on page 3, echoed on the matrix on page 6). Communicative effectiveness is largely met: titles conclude rather than label ('78% of the portfolio is incremental — against a 50% target', 'Eleven projects, three years, zero revenue — close them now'), the page 4 chart carries a legend, axis label and an ambition-vs-reality note, and the page 10 table carries €M/yr units and a caveat line. Level 5 is not reached: page 5's two axis cards and page 11's three '01/02/03' rule cards leave roughly a third of the slide empty above the floating blue band, so the vertical rhythm breaks against the denser pages; the page 6 matrix is a plain rectangle with three flat circles and a blue sentence set like a hyperlink rather than a caption, which is the least crafted artefact in the deck; and page 3's five stat blocks are a stock KPI strip. On genericness: the content is specific to this portfolio, but the visual language — corporate blue, numbered blue boxes on page 2, bordered white cards, coloured action bars — is a default consulting shell that would survive a topic swap with only the words changed.

Integrity holds: no clipped or placeholder text is visible across the ten pages, and slide 10's three-card row and slide 7's criteria stack both render fully. Legibility is the first real strain — slide 8's table footnote and slide 7's criteria card body copy are set very small relative to everything else, and the white-on-orange 'Capability fit — 40%' card on slide 7 sits at borderline contrast; slide 3's table source line and the chart source lines on 4/5/6 are near the floor for projected type. Coherence is broadly good: the eyebrow label + assertive title pattern repeats on every page, the footer/page-number rule is consistent, and the A=blue / B=purple / C=orange colour coding is honoured in the charts on 4, 5, 6 and 9, in the table row chips on 3 and 8, and in the bullet squares on 2. Communicative effectiveness is where it stops short of 4. The bar charts on slides 4, 5, 6 and 9 all have a source line, but their takeaway lives only in the slide title — there is no takeaway caption on the plot itself, and slide 9's chart shows values 3.0/3.2/3.45-ish with no unit or scale label beyond 'Weighted score (1-5 basis)'; the y-axis on slide 4 is labelled 'EUR millions' but slide 5's axis is unlabelled with only the title carrying '%'. Slide 9's ordering (C, A, B) is right but the bar colour order breaks the A-B-C left-to-right convention used everywhere else, so the eye has to re-read the axis. Slide 7's donut has no data labels — the three weights (35/25/40) exist only in the left-hand cards, forcing a cross-reference. Slide 8's table crams four numeric columns plus a weighted score into a footnote-heavy block that repeats what slide 9 then charts, so two of ten slides carry one idea. Distinctiveness: the palette, the full-bleed navy title, the chip-coded rows and the three-card close are competent and consistently applied, but the arrangement is the standard consulting scan skeleton — title, comparison table, three single-metric bar charts, criteria, scored matrix, recommendation — and nothing in the composition is specific to these three segments beyond the numbers dropped into it. Not sendable unchanged: fix the missing chart takeaways/units, the small footnote and card type, and collapse the 8/9 duplication.

Integrity holds: no clipped, empty or placeholder blocks anywhere — the option cards on 4/5/6, the seven-row criteria table on 3, the comparison matrix on 7 and the risk table on 9 all render complete. Legibility is fine at ExCo scale, though the footnote lines under the chart on 8 and the disclaimer on 6 are near the floor. Coherence is strong: the green top rule, the uppercase eyebrow (CONTEXT / OUR APPROACH / OPTION 1 OF 3 — FULL AUTONOMY), the footer 'Group operating model review · Strictly confidential' and page number repeat exactly, and the three option slides share one skeleton (bullets left, stat card right). Communication is mostly there — titles conclude rather than label ('On every criterion, Option 3 is the pragmatic middle ground', 'Cost and risk move in opposite directions'), the recommended column on 7 and the Option 3 row on 9 are deliberately highlighted, and units carry through ('EUR m /yr' axis, 'EUR 9m / yr'). It stops short of level 5 on craft and on two specific defects. First, the chart on 8 plots +14 against -9 and -5 on a single axis and then explains in a footnote that 'negative values are annual net savings' — the reader has to read a note to know that the tallest bar is the bad outcome; the sign convention fights the takeaway title. Second, whitespace is unmanaged: the bottom 40% of slides 2, 4, 5 and 6 is empty below the stat card, and slide 12 leaves a large gap between the four approval bullets and 'Thank you — questions and discussion', so dense 8pt bullets sit beside acres of blank. Minor inconsistency too: slide 4's card reads 'EUR 14m' with no rate while 5 and 6 read 'EUR 9m / yr' and 'c. EUR 5m / yr', and only 6 hedges with 'c.'. Substantively it is written for this brief — eleven businesses, the EUR 14m/9m/5m ladder, the shared-service layer 'nobody currently runs' turned into a named risk on 9 — but the visual system (green accent rule, grey stat card, grey-header table) is a stock consulting shell that would carry any other topic unchanged.

Integrity holds: no visible clipping, empty frames or placeholder text across slides 1–12; the org charts on 5 and 6 and the two-column transition boxes on 11 all sit inside their frames. Legibility is the first real strain — the risk table on 12 runs three dense text columns plus a fourth 'Decisions needed today' callout at what looks like 6–7pt, and the 'What changes' column on slide 9 and the right column of the two-column table on 7 are similarly small; slide 4's tiny footnote ('Source: internal…') and the italic caption under 6 ('Delivery capacity is created and allocated…') are near-illegible at projection size. Coherence is largely met: the orange/blue accent pair, the eyebrow-label + sentence-title pattern, and the running footer repeat consistently on every page, and the KPI-tile treatment on 4 and 8 matches. Where it breaks down is craft and communicative effectiveness. Slides 4 and 8 restate the same figures — 900, 140, 11, 7 — in near-identical tile rows, so slide 8 adds nothing; the 'At a glance' box on slide 2 makes it a third repetition. Nothing in the deck is an actual chart: every quantitative page is a number tile or a text table, so a 900→140→11/7 flow, a cost-of-duplication comparison, or a two-quarter timeline all go unvisualised, which is the biggest missed opportunity for an org-design case. The 'Transition runs across two quarters' page (11) is two bulleted boxes of week ranges where a Gantt or swimlane belongs. Slide 3's segment/region chips are decorative rather than evidential — three coloured boxes over three grey boxes with the label 'today's structure doesn't match this' carries no data. Slide 10 is a plain bulleted list of eleven role titles with no visual weight despite being the most politically loaded page for this audience. Titles do mostly conclude rather than label ('Our customers don't buy by region — but we're organised as if they do' on 3, 'Three parallel regional models carry a cost we can now see clearly' on 4), which is a genuine strength. But units are inconsistent: '62–91%' on slide 4 has no denominator visible in the tile, '3x' and '5.5 wks' lack a stated baseline, and only slide 4 carries a source line. Genericness: the sentence-title-plus-eyebrow system and the sober blue/orange palette are competent but are the default consulting-deck skin; swap the words and this same file serves a pricing review or a systems migration unchanged. Not something I'd put my name on without rebuilding 8, 10 and 11 and shrinking the text on 12.

Integrity holds: no clipped cells, no lorem, no empty frames. The four KPI cards on p2 (118 / 94 / 17 / 7) all resolve, the p3 donut renders with a legend, the p4 at-risk table fits eight rows without spill, and the p6 three-card row is evenly gutted. Legibility is fine everywhere except p8, where the milestone captions under the gantt segments ('Legal notices & registrar', 'Works council final', 'Customer comms signed', 'Payroll parallel test run'…) are set several points below any other body text on the deck and are packed under narrow bars — readable in a leave-behind, marginal projected. The p6 card body ('RISK IF UNRESOLVED' / 'PATH TO GREEN' / 'OWNER') is the second-smallest type. Coherence is strong and clearly systematic: the uppercase eyebrow + blue conclusion headline + hairline rule repeats on every content page, the footer is identical, and the red/amber/green semantics are consistent from the p3 status table through the p4 Type chips, p5 blocker names, p7 status column and p8 bar colours. Communicative effectiveness is where this deck earns its level: titles are conclusions, not labels ('Three blockers stand between us and a clean Day One', 'Four items are escalated for Steering Committee decision'), each exhibit carries a takeaway line beneath it, the p3 table has a 'What it means' column rather than bare counts, and p9 gives every escalation a decision maker and a needed-by date. What stops it at 4 rather than 5: the p8 timeline is the one hand-fought exhibit — segment widths do not encode duration consistently and the caption band under it is cramped compared with the generous whitespace on p6 and p10; p10's lower half is thin, with four short bullets and a large dark date banner doing the work of a closing page; and the p4 Type column uses solid red/orange fills that read heavier than the same states rendered as coloured text on p7, so the same semantic is expressed two ways. On genericness: the content is unmistakably this brief — 340 transferring staff, the German works council, the named VP Comms and HR Lead owners, the 18 September gate — but the visual language (navy/blue headline, grey banded tables, red callout strip) is standard consulting-deck issue and would look identical on any other status readout.

Integrity holds: no clipped or empty frames, no placeholder text, and the three account tables (8, 9, 10) all fill. Legibility is the first real crack — the four-card rows on slides 4, 6 and 14 set body copy at a size that is fine on a laptop but marginal projected in a workshop room, and slide 3's chevron labels ('Cost to serve', 'Standard margin', 'Discount stag (5%)') are set inside coloured arrows at what looks like 7–8pt, effectively unreadable from the back of a room in a deck explicitly built to be talked through. Coherence is largely met: the blue/grey palette, left-aligned blue titles, one-line deck, and the repeated grey-header two-column table pattern on 5, 8, 9, 10 and 15 do repeat faithfully, and the two dividers (7, 12) match each other. Where it stops short of level 4 is communicative: the charts carry no source or unit line — slide 11's bars are labelled 40,000/46,000 etc. with no currency and no note that they are annual contract value; slide 13's axis reads $0–$2,500 with the takeaway buried in the subtitle ('Median monthly willingness to pay by usage segment, n=406') rather than stated as a conclusion; and slide 11's title 'Value-based pricing isn't just charge more' is a claim the chart supports but the chart itself has no takeaway caption. Slide 3's chevron is decorative rather than informative — five arrows convey a sequence the body text already states. The metric cards on 3 ('21%', '3 tiers', '0') are the strongest single device in the deck. Genericness sits at moderate: the content is unmistakably this brief (account A/B/C worked examples, the n=406 survey, the named decisions and owners on 15), but the containers — grey card rows, chevron process bar, header-band tables, full-bleed blue divider — are stock consulting furniture that would carry any topic unchanged. Nothing here is wrong; it is competent and unremarkable, and the small chevron type alone would keep me from sending it out with my name on it.

Integrity holds: no clipped text, no placeholder strings, every page carries real content. Legibility is adequate at presentation size, though slide 3's four mini-charts push axis values and the -2.5%/-20% annotations to near-illegible sizes, and the body bullets on slides 4-7 are small relative to the empty space beside them. Coherence is the deck's strength — the eyebrow label, blue conclusion title, right-hand variance badge and Actual/Plan bar pair repeat identically across slides 4-7, and the card grids on 9, 10 and 11 share a common gutter and radius. Where it stops is communicative effectiveness. Slides 4, 5, 6 and 7 each spend a full chart on a single two-bar comparison, and the axes are truncated: on slide 5 the 18.2% vs 17.5% bars differ in height by roughly half, visually inflating a 0.7pt beat, and slide 7 does the same to 312 vs 325. No chart on any page carries a source line, and none carries a takeaway caption under the plot — the conclusion lives only in the title. Slide 2 leaves a large blank band between the six-bullet block and the 'Asking today' line, and slide 12 leaves an even larger one above 'Thank you — questions and discussion', so both read as under-filled rather than deliberately airy. Slide 8's donut splits five initiatives into five slices, which is a lot of chart for a 2/2/1 count. On distinctiveness: the blue-on-white palette, the grey rounded cards, the numbered 1-4 grid on slide 10 and the KPI strip on slide 12 are the standard consulting deck kit; swap the numbers and this would serve any business unit in any quarter. Nothing here is wrong enough to embarrass, but the truncated axes and missing sources are enough that I would not put my name on it unchanged.

Integrity holds: no clipping, no lorem, every card on slides 3, 6 and 10 is filled. Legibility is adequate but thinnest on slide 5, where the two 'Script & QA rewrite' / 'Pay & incentive review' cards carry four stacked micro-labelled paragraphs (What we did / What happened / What it missed) at what looks like 9pt, and on slide 4 where the three driver boxes ('Turnover 44%', 'First-contact resolution 54%', 'Handling time +38%') set explanatory text smaller than anything else in the deck. Coherence is the deck's strongest suit: the eyebrow label, the rule under the title, the blue heading and the footer repeat exactly on all twelve pages, and slides 7-9 are a genuine triptych — same bullet column, same right-hand 'PRIMARY TARGET' block with today / 6 months / 12 months. Communicatively it mostly works: titles conclude rather than label ('NPS fell because three operating metrics moved together', 'Three levers, moved together and in order'), the slide 11 table carries baseline, 6- and 12-month targets, a primary-owner column and units on every figure, and slide 12 converts the plan into three named approvals. Two things stop it short of level 5. First, the central claim — that the three metrics are one reinforcing loop — is drawn on slide 4 as three boxes in a left-to-right row with a caption saying 'which feeds back into turnover', not as a loop; the diagram contradicts its own title. Second, an eighteen-month fall from 41 to 12 is never plotted: slide 3 states '12' as a static card and the deck contains no chart at all, so the trend the board is being asked to reverse is asserted in text only. Minor: the slide 3 title wraps onto a second line ('...driving it down') that crowds the 'THE SCOREBOARD' section label beneath it, and slide 10's four milestone columns leave a deep unused band under the shortest column. On genericness, the content is unmistakably built for this brief — 41→12, 54% FCR, +38% AHT, 44% attrition recur as the spine — but the visual language (grey stat blocks, numbered circles, thin coloured left rules) is stock consulting furniture that would survive a find-and-replace into any other turnaround deck.

Integrity holds: no empty frames, no visible placeholder text, and the twelve slides are all populated. Legibility is where the deck starts to strain — the body text on 2, 5, 7, 9, 10, 11 and 12 is set very small relative to the titles (the three-column stat band on 2 and the 'What it does' bullets on 9–11 are near the floor for a projected deck), and the axis/label type on the charts (4, 6, 12) plus the footnote lines under 5 and 8 are smaller still. The stacked footnotes on 5 ('Actives (moved >6 months)... Obsolete items tracked as a subset...') read as fine print that will be unreadable in a room. Coherence is genuinely good and is the level earned: consistent left-rail title block, running footer 'Supply Chain Inventory Diagnostic — Confidential' with page number on every slide, an eyebrow label system ('WHERE — THE GAP TO BENCHMARK', 'INTERVENTION 1 OF 3'), and a repeated numbered-badge + boxed-metric motif on 9/10/11 that makes the three interventions read as a set. Communicative effectiveness falls short of level 4 in specific places: titles do state conclusions ('38% of inventory hasn't moved in six months; a third of that is already obsolete', 'Liquidating obsolete stock alone releases EUR 4.9m within 90 days'), which is the strongest thing here, but the charts are inconsistently supported — slide 4's bar pair and slide 12's waterfall-style bars carry no source line while slide 5 and 6 do; slide 6's two-bar 'Current vs Workable baseline' comparison is a wasteful use of a full chart for two numbers and its y-axis label is unreadable; slide 12's bar labels (94, 34, 30, 60) sit without a visible unit on the axis. Slide 8's table is the weakest page: five narrow columns with a 'Difficulty' column of one-word values and an asterisked footnote doing real definitional work in agate type, and the 'Medium*' cell carrying a caveat the reader cannot resolve at size. Slide 7's four-box causal chain is the most considered artifact in the deck but its box copy is set smaller than any other body text on the page. Craft is competent monochrome-plus-grey but the pie on 5 with its heavy legend-and-footnote apparatus, and the near-identical construction of 9/10/11, read as three passes through one layout rather than three arguments. Not something I would put my name on unchanged — I would rebuild slide 8, kill the chart on 6, and lift every body size a step.

On genericness: it is not a blank template — the eyebrow labels, the numbered intervention badges, and the causal-chain graphic on 7 are shaped to this specific inventory argument, and the titles carry findings rather than topics. But the visual language (black/grey/white, single serif-free title, boxed metrics) would transfer unchanged to any cost or margin diagnostic; nothing about the palette, the chart forms or the composition says 'supply chain' or says this firm.

Integrity holds — no clipped or placeholder text visible, and the deck covers the brief (baseline p2, target p3, lever table p4, four lever pages p5-p8, gap p9, decisions p10). Legibility is mostly fine, though the p4 lever table and the p10 decisions table are set in very small type for a projected slide, and the p3 chart's y-axis gridline labels (0–90,000) are near-illegible at slide scale. Coherence is the deck's strength: the blue rule under every title, the left-aligned title, the footer with page number, and the KPI-card + bullet pattern repeat consistently across p5-p8.

Where it fails level 4: the four lever slides (p5, p6, p7, p8) are the same layout four times with only the number and colour changed, and each wastes roughly two-thirds of the canvas — a grey card holding one figure floats left of three short bullets with an enormous empty band beneath. That's four slides carrying about one slide of content, and the grey fill reads as an unstyled placeholder box rather than a designed panel. The p3 bar chart is two bars where a waterfall or pathway line was the obvious choice for a 'pathway to 2030' — it shows the endpoints but not the trajectory the brief asked for, and the four levers never appear as a bridge from 84,000 to 48,720. Chart takeaways and sources are inconsistent: p2's donut has a small caveat line, p3 and the p4 table have footnotes, but nothing carries a real source attribution and the p3 chart has no takeaway beneath it. The p9 gap slide is the strongest page — three cards with a genuine argument in the italic line below — but the '20 of 44' card reuses the same three-metric card shape as the others for a fundamentally different kind of claim.

Genericness: the palette is default-Office blue with a green and an amber accent, the type is a stock sans, and apart from the coloured KPI numerals there is no visual idea specific to decarbonisation or to this company. Swap the words and this is any corporate roadmap deck.

Integrity holds: no clipped, overlapping, or placeholder content anywhere in the five pages; the comparison table on p3 renders all six rows fully within its column widths. Legibility holds: single-column measure, consistent black-on-white, obvious top-to-bottom order. Coherence largely holds too — the H2 rule under 'Executive Summary', 'The Situation', 'Risks to Manage' and 'Recommended Next Steps' is the same weight throughout, the meta block on p1 (Prepared for / Date / Status) is consistently styled, and the p1 stat row (4pts / 38% / 61%) is the one deliberate typographic moment. It fails at level 4 on flow and density. The 'What Would Change This Recommendation' list on p4 breaks mid-item, so p5 opens with four orphaned bullets ('switching back, that is direct evidence…') under no heading — a reader landing on p5 cannot tell what list they are in. p2 stops after the single Option A paragraph with roughly the bottom 45% of the page blank, and p5 has a similar dead band between the orphaned bullets and 'Recommended Next Steps', plus an empty lower third; that is unmanaged pagination, not intentional breathing room. Content-wise it is also under-structured for the brief: Option A gets a plain prose paragraph on p2 while Option B gets prose plus the table on p3, so the two options are not presented symmetrically, and the 4pts/38%/61% figures appear only as p1 callouts with no chart or trend anywhere to carry the three-year share erosion. The 'Recommendation' heading on p3 is a label, not a conclusion, although the sentence beneath it does state the call. On genericness: strip the words and this is a default Word report — one table, one stat row, no colour, no rule system beyond the heading underline, nothing that says heritage food brand or that could not be reused verbatim for a telecom or insurance assessment.

Integrity fails on the tables. Page 1's 'Where the shortfall sits' table: the header row runs 'Delivered vs.Status target' — the 'Delivered vs. target' and 'Status' headers have collided into one cell with no space, and the Procurement row shows '118%Ahead of plan' with the same collision. The IT row's 'What's blocking it' cell reads 'Legacy-platform retirement decision not' and is cut off mid-sentence at the page edge with no continuation. Page 2 repeats the same broken header ('Delivered vs.Status target') with an orphaned 'taken' fragment sitting alone in the row below — that is the tail of page 1's clipped IT cell, so the table has split badly across the page break and left the header repeating over a one-word remnant. Page 2's decisions table has the same run-together problem in the third row: 'Name a single accountable owner for the Property and IT workstreams at Steering Committee' collides with 'Programme Sponsor (Transformation SRO)' and 'Next Steering Committee' with no cell separation, so owner and deadline are unreadable as distinct fields. Page 3 opens with a two-word orphan ('different workstream.') above the section 3 heading. The KPI strip on page 1 (EUR46m / EUR19m / EUR28m / 68%) is the one well-made element — labelled, unit-bearing, aligned — but a single good band cannot lift a document whose primary evidence tables are clipped and mis-columned. Content-wise the brief is answered (decisions, owners, deadlines, recovery values, the do-nothing landing of EUR41-43m), which makes the rendering failure more costly, not less. Genericness: the type is undifferentiated body serif with plain rules, no brand mark, no colour, no distinguishing device beyond the number band; swap the words and this is any consultancy memo.

Integrity holds: three pages, no clipped or placeholder text, the page 1 cohort table (Full-price joins 68%/32%, Promotional-price joins 41%/59%) renders fully, and page 3 ends on a completed recommendation rather than a cut sentence. Legibility is fine for a screen-read docx — the 5.9%/41%/68%/$1.5M stat row and the 2,250/$124K/$1.5M row on page 2 are the only large type, body text is dark on white. Coherence is where it plateaus rather than fails: the two stat bands use the same treatment but different caption lengths, so the '+2.5 pts vs. 4 quarters ago / Current monthly churn' block on page 1 runs to four lines while its neighbours run to two, leaving a ragged baseline under an otherwise aligned row; and page 3 opens mid-document with a numbered heading ('2. Replace gross sign-ups with a retention-weighted acquisition metric') and no page-level anchor, so the eye has nothing to land on. Level 4 is not met: the document is essentially three columns of running prose with one table and two number rows, and the single most important relationship in the brief — 41% vs 68% vs the four-point gap at staffed-onboarding sites — is never drawn, only tabulated and then re-narrated in paragraphs. The cohort table carries no source line and its '12-Month Retention'/'12-Month Churn' columns are unitless percentages with no denominator (how many sites, how many members). The $1.5M 'Revenue at stake' figure appears twice, on page 1 and page 2, with no cross-reference and a hedge buried in the page 2 paragraph that the figure 'assumes nothing changes' — that caveat belongs adjacent to the number, not four lines below it. Titles are honest ('Member Churn Diagnosis: From 3.4% to 5.9% in Four Quarters', 'Revenue at Stake Over the Next Four Quarters') but sectional rather than concluding; 'What's Actually Happening' and 'What We Recommend' are labels, not findings. Distinctiveness is low: black-on-white, one accent, a plain ruled table, and a stat row that would read identically for a SaaS or insurance brief — nothing here is specific to a 140-site fitness chain beyond the words.

Integrity mostly holds — no clipped text or placeholders visible — but page 6 is a near-empty orphan carrying a single two-line closing paragraph at the very top of an otherwise blank page, which reads as an accident of pagination rather than an intended closing page. Page 2 also breaks badly: the numbered executive-summary items 3 and 4 are stranded at the top, detached from items 1-2 on page 1, with no continuation cue. Legibility is adequate for A4 print though the running body text is set small and dense, and the small grey captions under the three big stats on page 1 ('of new motor policies sold through brokers today') are noticeably light. Coherence is generally good: consistent heading weights, a repeated table style, and the 78%/57%/9% stat row on page 1 is a genuine composed element. But two things look hand-placed: the oversized 'Year 3 / +EUR 9,000' display block on page 3 sits at a scale used nowhere else in the document, and the two tables on page 3 are stacked with no gap or heading between them so the second table's header row ('Period | Gross saving vs today | Transition investment | Net effect') reads as a continuation of the first. Communicative effectiveness is where it stops: for a document whose whole argument is a three-year cost curve, there is not a single chart — the payback story on page 3 is carried entirely by two adjacent tables, and the reader has to do the arithmetic to see the crossover. Table headers do carry currency units (EUR), which is good, but no table has a source line or a takeaway caption. Section headings are descriptive labels ('Where the economics stand today', 'The three-year channel mix', 'What the investment buys') rather than conclusions, though 'Year 2 — make brokers users of the engine, not competitors to it' on page 4 is a real exception and shows what the rest could have been. The brief's core question — the year the shift starts making money — is answered, and the Year 1/2/3 broker-relationship narrative on page 4 is specific and non-generic prose. Genericness is moderate rather than high: the content is clearly written for this insurer, but the shell is a plain single-column Word report with a serif-free stack and no visual identity beyond the stat row.

Integrity holds: no clipped text, no placeholder strings, and the two tables (p3 ESRS topic readiness, p7 milestone/target) sit inside their frames. Legibility is the first real weakness — the body column on pages 2, 4, 5, 6 and 8 runs at a very small size across a narrow measure with generous surrounding white space, and page 4's 'Scope 3 Emissions Gap' section is four dense unbroken paragraphs of that small type with no entry point. Coherence is mostly met: the same left-aligned heading style, the same rule under section titles, and the same one-column measure repeat page to page. But the page-1 statistic band (34 of 82 / 29 of 82 / 19 of 82) is the single strongest device in the document and never returns — the same three numbers reappear on page 3 only as a table row and on page 4 only inside prose, so the design's one distinctive element reads as hand-placed rather than systematic. Communicative effectiveness fails in specific places: the p3 table title 'Datapoint Readiness Assessment' states the subject, not the conclusion (the finding is that all 11 Scope 3 datapoints are in the 'needs new measurement' column, which the reader must derive by scanning); no figure anywhere carries a source line or a note on the 82-datapoint basis, which is deferred to the p8 'Assumptions' bullets; and the emissions discussion on p4 mentions 750 employees and 1,400 employees in running text with no chart or comparison to anchor it. Pages 2, 5 and 6 are wall-to-wall prose and bullets for an audit committee brief, where the readiness split, the Scope 3 gap and the timeline all wanted visual treatment — only the timeline got a table. Genericness: the palette is default black-on-white with a single grey table header, the type is a stock serif/sans pairing, and apart from the p1 number band this would look identical as a tax memo or an IT audit; the CSRD subject matter shows only in the words.

Integrity holds: no clipped or placeholder content on any of the four pages, and the numbered conditions that break from page 3 to page 4 continue cleanly. Legibility is adequate for a printed board memo, though the page 2 bar chart's category labels (Year 0 through Year 4) and both chart footnotes sit at the low end of readable, and the page 3 line chart's two-unit tick labels across 0–36 crowd the axis. Coherence is real and repeats: the same rule-under-title treatment, the same three-up big-number band on page 1 (EUR 340m / 61% / 0) and page 2 (EUR 2.1m / Month 26 / Month 34), the same confidentiality footer on every page. Where it stops short of level 4 is craft in the exhibits: the page 2 right-hand chart title breaks mid-word as 'concentra-tion' across three lines, the pie sits small inside an over-wide plot box with its legend crammed against it, and the two side-by-side charts are visibly unequal in optical weight; the payback table below appears to sit wider than the body text column it should align to. Content-wise it is strong for the brief — chart titles are conclusions ('Incumbent concentration leaves room to enter'), each has an illustrative-basis note, units are stated, and both scenarios are shown in the table and the cash-position chart. Page 4 ends with roughly half the page empty, which is acceptable as a closing page but leaves the document ending flat. Not shippable unchanged because of the hyphenated chart heading and the unbalanced page 2 exhibit pair. Genericness: the numbers and the Finnish-language gap argument are specific to this brief, but the visual language — Word-default serif-free body, one dark accent, boxed charts — would look identical for any other market-entry memo.

Page 7 is entirely blank — a trailing empty page ends the document, which is an integrity failure before any higher bar can be considered. Page 5 also breaks integrity of composition: the big '€3.3m ▼' stat sits alone with a caption, then a two-row table repeating the same €3.3m fact immediately below, and the page ends with a table fragment that appears cut mid-thought and continues on page 6 with a headerless continuation row starting 'captured, not a shift in timing' — the table header ('Area' / 'Effect of a 12-month deferral') is repeated on page 6 but the first data cell has been orphaned across the break, so the reader sees a dangling sentence with no row label. Page 1's KPI strip is the strongest element (31% / 29% / €8.2m / 40% with legible sub-labels), but its caption text runs to different depths under each figure and the fourth caption wraps to five lines against the first's two, so the strip's baseline rhythm collapses. Page 3's phase headings ('Phase 1 — Stabilise, decide and harvest…', 'Phase 2 — Fund and mobilise…') are good conclusion-bearing titles, and page 4's milestone table with a 'Definition of done' column is genuinely useful and specific to the brief. Colour is essentially absent — a single accent rule under the title on page 1 and nothing else — so the document reads as a default Word report with the brief's numbers typed in; the synergy composition table on page 2 (€4.9m / €3.3m / €8.2m with share and 'What unlocks it') carries all the analytical weight with no visual treatment at all. Nothing on the deferral cost is charted, despite that being the single decision the steering committee must make.

Integrity and legibility hold: no placeholders, no clipped text, and the two-column memo block (To/From/Date/Re) on page 1 plus the numbered section spine (1. Where the Margin Went → 6. Modeled Outcome) give an obvious reading order. Typography and colour are consistent — black-filled table header rows on pages 2, 3, 4 and 5 all match, and the KPI stat rows (22%, 12pts, 0%, 52% on page 1; 26–27%, 8–10%, 100% on page 6) repeat the same numeral/caption pairing, so it bookends rather than looks hand-placed. Communicatively it does the job the brief asked: the segmentation table carries share of accounts, margin position and a 'Read' column; the Tier table on page 3 carries scope, action, timing and expected churn (26–30% / 6–9% / <2%) with units on every number; page 5 answers the refusal question with a six-step escalation playbook. What stops it short of craft-level is two page-break failures in tables: at the top of page 3 the repeated header row is followed by a near-empty row where only the tail of the 'Core (unmeasured)' Read cell ('account-level data says otherwise.') sits, columns blank to its left; the same happens at the top of page 5, where the runway table repeats its Window/Wave/Milestone header and then shows a row with an empty Window cell and an orphaned 'wave 1' fragment. Both read as breakage rather than continuation. Secondarily, a document whose whole argument is a 31%→19% margin slide over three years carries no chart at all — the decline and the three-tier runway are asserted in prose and grids only, and page 6's lower third is left blank. Content is unmistakably written for this parcel-carrier brief, not swapped into a shell.

Integrity fails on the orphan pages. Page 3 contains only two stranded lines of body text ('volume, with no visibility into what a sister property pays...') at the very top and is otherwise blank; page 5 is likewise a near-empty page holding two leftover bullets (facilities maintenance & engineering, IT/telecom & software) plus a closing sentence; page 7 is almost entirely white with a single half-sentence fragment ('materially, because they are built from the concentration and variance findings...'); page 9 repeats the pattern with two lines at the top ('At steady state, the programme costs about 1% of the spend it manages...') and nothing else. That is four of ten pages given over to two-line widows — content that clearly overflowed the preceding page rather than being placed. Page 6 also splits its own heading region oddly: 'The addressable saving, and what we will actually capture' sits with a large KPI row (6.4€m / 1.9€m / 6.0–6.5€m / ~7%) and a three-row capture table, then dumps its conclusion onto page 7. Beyond that, the underlying work is decent — the page-4 category prioritisation table with spend, share, price variance, saving % and wave, and the page-8 cost-to-run table with FTE and annual cost — but the rubric does not let those compensate. On genericness: the KPI-strip-plus-table pattern is a recognisable consulting-memo template, but the numbers, the eight-category wave sequencing and the 4.0 FTE + platform cost build are specific to this brief, so it is not interchangeable boilerplate; it is a stock layout carrying real content.

Integrity holds: no clipped or placeholder blocks are visible across the ten pages; tables on p2 (channel unit economics), p3 (segment share), p7 (transition cost), p8 and p9 (risk/mitigation) all sit inside their columns, and the page-10 fragment is short but intentional (two closing bullets, not an orphaned heading). Legibility is adequate for a printed board paper, though the wall-of-text body on pages 4, 5, 6, 8 and 10 runs long-measure at what looks like 9pt with no visual relief for pages at a stretch. Coherence is mostly there — the same serif-free heading treatment, the same rule under section titles, the same two-column risk table styling on p8 and p9 — but it breaks in two places: the page-2 KPI block (210,000 / 6.40 / 44% / 24.80 / 434,700 / 667,000 / ~25 months) is a floating six-up numeric panel with mixed unit sizes and a stray upward arrow that appears nowhere else in the document, and the page-1 metadata line ('Prepared for / Subject / Date') is set in a small italic run that no other page echoes. Level 4 fails: there is not a single chart anywhere in a document whose whole argument is a cost distribution — counters at 8% of contacts and 31% of cost is the headline finding and it is left as a table row on p2 and prose on p3; the year-1/year-2 saving ramp on p7 is a three-row table where a bridge would carry it. Section titles are also mostly topical ('The cost of contact today', 'Transition cost and payback', 'The financial case') rather than conclusive, and several tables (p3 segment table, p7 investment area) carry no source note. Genericness: the content is unmistakably this brief — the tier 1/2/3 model, the accessibility carve-out on p5 ('Passengers who lose access if counters close', six numbered passenger categories) and p6 ('How the redesigned model protects access') are real, specific work — but the container is a plain single-column Word report with a KPI strip; drop in different numbers and it would look identical. Not shippable as-is with my name on it, chiefly for the absent visual argument.

Integrity holds: no clipped text, no placeholders, no overflow across all five pages; tables on p2, p3 and p4 fit the measure and the metric rows on p3 top and p2 bottom are complete. Legibility is adequate but marginal — body copy on p5 (the seven numbered lease criteria and the four governance steps) is set very small and dense, running as a near-unbroken grey block with no visual relief for a page that is the operative decision rulebook. Visual coherence is the ceiling reached: a consistent single-column measure, a repeated rule-under-heading treatment, consistent table header shading (p2 segment table, p3 metric table, p4 store-group table), and the two KPI strips (p1: 212 / 62 / 18 / EUR 4.9m; p3: 21 / 33.9% / 9.9%) share the same numeral-over-caption form. Level 4 fails on several counts: page headings are topic labels, not conclusions — 'Where the estate stands today' (p2) and 'Criteria for the remaining lease decisions' (p5) state subject rather than finding, and only p3's 'The 21 sole-catchment stores are not on the closure list' actually concludes; the p4 online-demand section, which the brief asked for explicitly, is a three-row qualitative table plus two long paragraphs with no quantification of the leakage it discusses, while the 45% leakage figure sits orphaned in the p2 table; and the document has no chart anywhere — the 62/18/21 segmentation and the three-year lease-expiry profile are the two most obviously visual arguments in the brief and both are left as prose and tables. Craft: p4 and p5 are wall-of-text pages with no compositional idea, and the KPI strip appears twice with no third use, so it reads as an inserted device rather than a system. Genericness: the structure (exec summary, KPI strip, recommendation, criteria list, governance next steps) is the default consulting memo skeleton; strip the store numbers and the same pages would serve any cost-reduction brief. Nothing in the typography, colour (entirely black on white with grey rules) or layout is specific to a retail estate decision.

Integrity fails in two visible places. On page 1 the "Contents" heading at the foot of the cover has nothing beneath it — an unpopulated table of contents left as an empty section, which is the first thing a board member sees. On page 3 the Exposure Assessment table's header row collides: "Components" wraps as "Componen/ts" and the last two headers run together as "ShareNotes", with body cells doing the same ("35%No qualified second source in active use", "79% ofRequires new qualification", "65%Assumed resilient baseline") — the Share column has no gutter against Notes, so a percentage and a sentence read as one string. That is a broken column, not a tight one. Beyond that, pacing is uneven: page 2 ends at roughly half height, page 3 at half, and page 6 carries only the four numbered board decisions and an owner line on an otherwise blank sheet, while "Governance and Next Steps" is stranded at the bottom of page 5 with a single orphan line of intro. The Tier Summary table on page 5 is squeezed into five narrow columns where nearly every cell wraps to three or four lines. What works: the four-up stat band on page 1 (260 / 91 / 19 / 11 days) and the paired 1.4% / 63% figures on page 3 are well-set with units and captions, the three-tier recommendation structure directly answers the brief's now/qualify/accept ask, and headings like "The Financial Case for Dual-Sourcing the Top 20" state a conclusion rather than a topic. Visually it is a competent but anonymous serif consulting memo — no chart anywhere despite a modelled-downtime argument that begs for one, no colour beyond a grey table header, and nothing in the composition that ties it to a component-supply incident rather than any other board paper.

Integrity holds: no clipped text, no placeholders, no overlaps across the seven pages. Legibility is adequate but marginal — the body text on pages 3, 4 and 7 is set at a noticeably smaller size than the body on pages 1, 2 and 5-6, and page 7's opening bullets sit at the same small size as page 4's, so the type scale is not stable across the document. Coherence is mostly there — consistent left-aligned heading style, consistent three-rule table style on pages 2, 3, 5 and 6 — but two failures keep it from clearing level 4. First, page breaks are handled poorly: page 4 opens mid-bullet with an orphaned 'Review attrition by tenure band and BU rate by level quarterly' fragment carried over onto page 5, and page 6 opens with an orphaned table fragment ('Recruiting capacity & junior pipeline / Total') detached from the 'The plan's own cost' table that begins at the bottom of page 5, so the same table is split with its header on one page and two rows alone on the next. Page 7 similarly opens with three stranded assumption bullets separated from the 'Key assumptions' heading on page 6. Second, the brief asks to show the headcount bridge and the cost against run rate, and the document answers entirely in prose and plain tables — there is not a single chart anywhere in seven pages. The headcount bridge (240 → 400) and the retention-vs-hiring gap are exactly the material that should be a waterfall or stacked bar; instead the reader gets the page 2 five-column table and the page 3 three-row table, both of which are correct but make the partner do the arithmetic. The one visual moment, the four-stat KPI row on page 1 (67%, 26%, 62%, 116), is well-executed and unit-labelled, but it is never repeated, so it reads as a one-off rather than a system. Tables are also inconsistent: the page 2 bridge table has a 'Net change' column with +40/+55/+65 while the page 5 run-rate table crams three parenthetical deltas into single cells ('+160 (+66.7%)', '~$8,000 (-5.3%)', '+$20.8M (+57.8%)'), which is dense to the point of being hard to parse. Genericness: the content is specific to the brief — real tenure bands, the 62% fill rate, the junior:senior pyramid argument, a costed recommendation — but the presentation is default Word: single column, black on white, one accent-free type family, no theme colour, no rule or device that says 'engineering consultancy' or even 'this firm'. Strip the words and this is a page shell that would carry any topic unchanged.

I would not send this to a client unchanged: fix the four orphaned fragments at the page 3/4, 4/5, 5/6 and 6/7 boundaries, keep the cost table intact on one page, normalise the body size between pages 1-2 and 3-4-7, and turn the headcount bridge into an actual bridge chart.

Integrity fails first, so nothing above it counts. Page 1 ends with a bold 'Contents' heading and nothing beneath it — an empty/unpopulated table of contents left in the document. The severity tables break badly across pages: page 5 opens mid-row with an orphaned fragment ('as an SVG with submits no accessible payment; name; assistive technology announces it as a "button"'), and pages 7, 10 and 12 continue long tables with no repeated header row, so columns like Issue/Impact/Effort/Owner are unlabelled for a full page of rows. On page 4 the Impact and Shared-component columns are so narrow that cells wrap to one or two words per line ('Yes — Input', 'Yes — Date Picker'), and on page 5 the Issue/Impact text visually interleaves so it is hard to tell which sentence belongs to which cell. Legibility is also marginal: the findings tables are set several points smaller than body text and are near-unreadable at page scale, and the page-1 KPI strip (22 / 6 / 14 / 11) sits under labels of unequal width so the numbers do not line up with 'Journeys Tested', 'Blockers', 'Serious', 'Moderate'. Content-wise the substance is there — scope, exclusions, per-finding success criteria, remediation with effort and owner, retest plan, Appendix A SC index — but the presentation is unstyled Word default throughout: one typeface, no colour, no severity coding (blockers, serious and moderate rows look identical), no rule or accent anywhere, no header/footer or page numbering visible. It would look exactly the same for a procurement report or a security review; nothing on any page says accessibility audit, and ironically a report about visual accessibility uses type sizes and column widths that fail the readability it is auditing.

Integrity fails on page 1: the "Table of Contents" heading is followed by nothing — an empty field where the brief explicitly asked for a TOC — and section 1 starts immediately beneath it. Page 7 is a wholly blank trailing page. Those two alone cap the document at level 1 regardless of what happens above.

Beyond that, the vertical rhythm is broken by unmanaged white space: page 1 ends after a single executive-summary paragraph with ~40% of the page empty; page 2 ends after the one-sentence lead-in to "3. Options Evaluated"; page 4 ends after the two-line intro to "6. Migration Path" with the whole lower half blank; page 5 has an unexplained gap between the end of the Phase 0–5 list and the "7. Rollback Plan" heading. The phase list on page 5 is also orphaned from its parent heading (section 6 sits on page 4, its list on page 5).

Credits where due: the cost/performance table on page 3 is well built — every cell carries a unit (4,200 req/s, 180 ms, ~192 ms (180ms + 12ms measured overhead), EUR 3,800/month, 9/11 direct equivalents), and the header row correctly repeats at the top of page 4 where it splits. The three-stat band on page 1 (4,200 req/s / 180 ms / 1.5 eng-days/mo) is the one composed moment in the document.

Genericness: apart from that stat band and the thin rule under the title, this is a default single-column report — plain rule-only tables, unstyled numbered lists, no chart anywhere despite a latency/cost comparison that begs for one. Swap the words and the shell fits any brief.

Page 6 is entirely blank — no heading, no body, nothing — sitting between the 'Recommended Changes' table on page 5 and 'What to Measure After These Changes' on page 7. That is an integrity failure on its own: content the author meant to place either fell out or the page-break logic left an orphan spread. Page 8 compounds it: it carries two stray sentences ('Recommended cadence: review all six metrics weekly...' through '...treated as a new, unrelated incident') with no heading and enormous empty space below, i.e. the tail of page 7's section spilled onto a page it does not belong to. Page 7's table also runs the 'Why it matters' column so narrow that every cell wraps to five or six lines ('Retries are a symptom, not a fix; a rising trend means flakiness is returning untreated'), forcing the table to consume the full column height while the right margin sits idle. Elsewhere there is real competence: the page 3 stage table with a 'Total measured 47 min / 100%' summary row, the page 5 before/after savings table totalling 47→16 min, and the big-number callouts (47 min, 10 min, 37 min on page 2; 31%, 6% on page 3) are correctly unit-labelled with captions. But those callout captions are set in a grey so light and small (e.g. 'Flaky-test failure rate, hidden by auto-retry') they are near-illegible, and the visual language is otherwise plain single-column Word: no chart anywhere despite a brief that is entirely about a time budget breakdown, which is the one thing a stacked bar would have shown instantly. Left-aligned callout numbers with acres of white to their right on pages 2 and 3 make those pages feel half-built. Nothing about the styling says 'CI audit' rather than 'generic report'; swap the words and it is any consulting memo.

Integrity holds: no clipped or placeholder content is visible, and the six pages all carry real text. Legibility is the first real problem — page 3's top block starts mid-sentence with a bulleted continuation of section 2.1's assumptions and no heading, so the reader hits an orphaned list before the '2.2 Quarterly Projection' heading; page 5 does the same, opening with the fragment 'engineering estimate that needs validation against the pipeline's actual storage-vs-age profile...' continuing 3.2 from page 4, and page 4's own table ('Month / Utilization of committed capacity / Note') starts at month 7 with no repeated header context, so the 76%–98% rows on page 3 and the 100%–125% rows on page 4 read as two unrelated tables. Body type is also set very small and tight relative to the generous outer margins, particularly in the four-column lever table on page 5, where cells like 'Reduces compute pressure; 60–90% cost cut on migrated jobs' wrap to five lines in a column barely wider than a word. Visual coherence is broadly met — consistent numbered section headings, a repeated two/three-column table style, a single accent colour on the page 1 stat row — so level 3 is earned. Level 4 fails: the page 1 stat band shows '47% / 38% / 71% / 7mo' with legible sublabels, but that is the only quantitative display in the whole document; the quarterly projection (indexed compute 108→138, storage 114→171) and the month-by-month utilization ramp from 76% to 125% are the two numbers a capacity forecast exists to show, and both are left as bare tables with no chart and no marked breach point at month seven. Section titles are also category labels ('2.2 Quarterly Projection', '3.4 Lever Comparison') rather than conclusions — none of them says the cluster breaches in month seven or that downsampling is the recommended lever. The index tables give no basis note explaining that Q0=100. Genericness: apart from the one accent-coloured stat row on page 1, the document is a default Word memo — left-aligned headings, plain hairline tables, no rule, no running header or page furniture — and the same shell would serve a budget memo or a hiring plan unchanged.

Integrity fails on two counts. Page 2 is a Table of Contents that contains only the heading 'Table of Contents' and a single repeated line of the same words — no entries, no page numbers. It is effectively an unpopulated field/placeholder occupying a full page of a governance document whose whole value is navigability across 16 pages and cross-references like 'Yes - Section 4.1' in the retention table. Second, the retention table breaks catastrophically across pages 6/7: page 7 repeats the full header row (#, Data Class, Description, Retention Period, Retention Trigger, Conflict) but carries only the orphaned fragment 'Retention) documents.' — a stranded half-cell from the page-6 row — followed by two lines of body prose and then three-quarters of an empty page. Page 10 has the same problem in prose form, opening mid-argument on 'Mitigation' with the rest of the page blank. Beyond that, the retention table on page 6 has badly proportioned columns: 'Website & Product Usage Analytics' and 'Employee Expense & Reimbursement Records' wrap to four and five lines while the Description column is squeezed so hard that 'Access, security, and application error logs across production systems' stacks one or two words per line, and 'Retention Trigger' entries wrap to three lines. The seven data classes, the 30-day-to-seven-year range, and the three conflicts resolved in 4.1-4.3 are all substantively there and correctly cross-referenced, and the Trigger/Justification/Approval-required triplet in Section 7 repeats consistently across 7.1-7.5 — so the writing and structure are sound. But the empty TOC and the shattered retention table are exactly the two artefacts a compliance reader touches first. Visually it is undifferentiated Word: black text on white, one serif-free family, no rule work, no accent colour, tables with default hairline borders. Defensible for a policy, but nothing marks it as this company's policy rather than any other's.

Integrity holds: no clipping or placeholders, and the timeline and remediation tables both repeat their header row across the page 2→3 and 3→4 breaks. Legibility is adequate though thin — the page 1 executive summary and the page 3 cause paragraphs are set at a small size in a full-measure single column with no lead-in emphasis, so they read as undifferentiated grey blocks. Coherence is where it stalls. In the page 2 timeline table the Time column has effectively no right gutter, so 'Diagnosis', 'Resolution' and 'Recovery & verification' collide with the timestamps beside them ('02:33–04:05Diagnosis', '04:50–05:14Recovery & verification'); the same table's Event column is wide while Time/Phase are starved. In the page 3 remediation table the Action column is roughly a quarter width, forcing six- and seven-line wraps ('Lower replication-lag alerting to warn at 15s and page at 30s...') and ballooning row heights, while Owner, Target and Status sit in near-empty columns. Column widths were not fitted to content in either table. Communicatively the substance is right — the page 1 impact band (1,842 / 214 / 4h 00m with labels), the numbered causes, owners and targets in remediation, and the well-titled 'What Would Have Made This a Ten-Minute Incident' close with a concrete ten-minute reconstruction — but the presentation is entirely monochrome body text plus rules, with page 4 sitting roughly half empty after the table remainder. Presentation-wise this would look identical for any incident, any company: no colour, no severity or status coding in the Status column, no visual treatment of the eleven-minute dual-write window that is the heart of the story.

Integrity holds: no clipped or placeholder text, and every page renders content the author intended. Page 4 is only about a third full, but that is a legitimate final page, not a failure. Legibility is adequate for body copy, though the three grey captions under the page 1 stat row ('Target peak traffic multiplier', 'Ceiling before any fix (Run 1)', 'Ceiling after post-fix (Run 2)') are set several steps smaller than anything else in the document and sit near the floor of comfortable reading, and the 'x' in 3.2x/2.4x/3.1x is rendered as a shrunken subscript-like glyph that reads as an artefact rather than a deliberate unit mark. Coherence is met: headings, spacing and the single accent colour repeat consistently across pages 1–4, and the section rhythm (Executive Summary / Method / Test Runs and Results / Bottlenecks Identified / Fixes and Expected Headroom / Readiness Determination) is stable. Level 4 is where it stops. The page 2 results table is the load-bearing artefact of the whole report and it is the weakest element: six columns squeezed into equal narrow widths so that the header 'Checkout p99 at Limiting Ceiling Resource' runs together ambiguously, and every data cell wraps to three or four lines ('Payments service connection pool, saturates at 200 concurrent connections' stacked inside one narrow cell). The single most important fact in the brief — p99 collapsing from 340ms to 4.1s at 2.4x, a hard cliff not a gradient — is buried as wrapped text in a cell and never given a chart, so the document tells the reader about a cliff it never shows. The bottleneck headings on pages 2–3 are labels ('1. Payments service connection pool exhaustion') rather than conclusions, unlike the readiness section which does state its verdict in bold. On distinctiveness, the stat row is the one bespoke gesture; the rest is a plain heading-and-paragraph Word report whose skeleton would survive unchanged for any other subject.

Integrity holds: on page 1 the four-column 'Options considered' table wraps every cell without clipping (the long 'Meets requirement (vendor-documented)' and 'Meets requirement (configurable retention)' cells expand their rows rather than spilling), and the page-1-to-page-2 break falls mid-paragraph in the Recommendation body with no orphaned fragment or placeholder text. Legibility is fine: body and bullets are comfortably sized, the table header row is a light tint with dark text, and the single-column reading order is unambiguous. Coherence is consistent — the same heading weight and colour on 'Requirements', 'Options considered', 'Recommendation' (p1) and 'What would change the answer' (p2), the same bullet indent, one rule under the title and one under the meta line. Communicatively it does the job the brief asked: the table carries units in the row labels ('Throughput (50,000 msg/s)', 'Monthly cost' with 'EUR 5,100 / month'), the Recommendation names Option C explicitly, and page 2 gives four explicit switch conditions (30,000 msg/s ceiling raised, EUR 1,100/month becoming outside budget, 60,000 msg/s scaling, compliance rule). What keeps it off level 5 is craft: page 2 stops just past halfway, leaving roughly the bottom 45% of the sheet blank with nothing to balance it, and the section headings are category labels ('Requirements', 'Recommendation') rather than the conclusions themselves — only 'What would change the answer' earns its title. Nothing is composed; the table is a plain grid with no emphasis on the recommended column, so the reader has to hunt for which option won. Generic because this exact page — title, rule, meta line, bulleted requirements, four-column comparison table, closing prose — would be indistinguishable if the subject were vendor selection for anything else; there is no visual cue tied to brokers, throughput or the decision itself.

Integrity holds: across all 9 pages I see no clipped tables, no empty cells left as placeholders, no overlapping blocks. The wide tables (p3 Definitions, p4 Log Field / RED Metrics, p6 Retention Periods, p7 Remediation gap table, p8 Rollout quarters) all wrap inside their column widths and the final page closes cleanly with a Version History table rather than trailing whitespace. Legibility is adequate but is the weakest link at the top end: the body text on p2 (Definitions), p5 (Naming Conventions prose) and especially the dense two-column-feel paragraphs on p4's right page and p9's opening block sits at a small size with tight leading, and several table cells (p6 Retention, p7 gap table) run at a noticeably smaller size than body copy — readable on screen, marginal in print. Coherence is genuinely good and consistent: the same thin salmon rule under every numbered H1 (Purpose and Scope, Definitions, Required Signals, Naming Conventions, Retention Periods, Current-State Baseline, Rollout Plan, Exemption Process, Compliance and Enforcement, Ownership and Change Control), the same pale-pink header row on every table, consistent numbering to two levels (3.1/3.2/3.3, 4.1/4.2/4.3, 7.1/7.2), and a Document Control block on p1 that matches the Version History block on p9. Communicatively it does the brief's job: the baseline numbers are actually stated as a gap table on p7 with current state, required state and deadline columns; retention on p6 gives explicit hot/archive/deletion durations with units (30 days, 13 months, 3 years); the exemption process on p8 is an enumerated 6-item request plus quarterly review; the rollout is split into 7.1 New (one quarter) and 7.2 Existing (Q1/Q2/Q3 milestones with exit criteria). Every requirement is implementable without asking a person. It stops short of level 5 because the craft is competent rather than distinctive — the composition is a single-column ragged stack of headings and full-width tables from p2 to p9 with no rhythm changes, no callouts for the MUST rules, no visual treatment of the three required signals despite them being the document's spine, and the p1 cover is a plain title over a metadata table rather than a designed opening. The Contents on p1 is also cut mid-list (ends at 4.3) and continues onto p2, which reads as an accident of flow rather than an intentional break. Genericness is moderate-low: the salmon accent, the RED-metrics tables with real Prometheus metric names (http_server_requests_total, http_server_request_duration_seconds), and the W3C traceparent/span_id specifics anchor it to this brief, but the underlying shell — title, doc-control table, numbered sections, pink-header tables — would look identical for a security policy or a data-retention standard.

Page 1 carries a bold "Contents" heading followed by roughly eight lines of empty space before "1. Overview and constraints" — an unpopulated table of contents. That is a visible empty/unrendered element on the cover page, which caps the document at level 1 regardless of what follows. Two lesser defects reinforce it: on page 3 the target-schema table breaks identifiers mid-token ("shipping_postalcod / e") because the Column column is too narrow for the longest name, and the failure-modes table that starts on page 10 continues onto page 11 without repeating its "Failure mode / Detection / Mitigation and response" header row, so page 11 opens with a bare orphaned fragment ("does not parse cleanly") whose columns are unlabelled — unlike the monitoring table on pages 9–10, which does repeat its header, so the treatment is inconsistent. Everything else is genuinely solid: the numbered heading scheme (1.–11., 5.1/5.2/5.3) is consistent, the four-figure stat strip on page 1 (1.4B rows, 6,000 writes/sec, 31 hours, 4 deploys) carries units and labels, the phase sections each pair Changes / Exit criteria / Rollback in the same order, and the rollback summary on page 9 and monitoring thresholds table give real numbers (p99 latency, 0.1% dual-write error rate, 5-second replica lag) rather than filler. Genericness is moderate: the stat strip and the schema/rollback/monitoring tables are shaped to this brief and could not be lifted wholesale into another document, but the page furniture — plain serif-ish body, hairline-ruled tables, no colour, no running head or phase marker to orient the reader across the four phases — is the default report shell rather than a considered identity for a migration runbook.

Integrity fails before anything else can be credited. Page 1 is completely blank — no title, no marks — and the actual cover ("Authentication Service / Security Review Report") sits on page 2, with its metadata block (Report date, Assessment period, Target system, Assessment type) stranded alone on page 3 under an orphaned horizontal rule and acres of white. That is an empty page plus a title page split across two sheets. Beyond that, the flow is riddled with mid-page voids: page 9 leaves the top third empty before the "H-2 — Password reset tokens are valid for 24 hours" heading; page 15 has two stub lines ("grant access to the service", the L-2 remediation paragraph) then a large gap before "L-3 — Password policy permits weak or repeated-character passwords" starts in the lower half; pages 11 (M-2), 12 (M-3) and 17 (Recommendations, three list items) each stop around 60% and leave the rest bare. Pages 6 and 7 open on orphaned fragments — "Remediation for the two high findings..." and three loose severity-definition bullets — that belong to the preceding page's block. The Summary of Findings table on page 7 is set to roughly half the text column, leaving a wide unexplained margin to its right while the body text beside it runs full measure, so repeated elements do not repeat. Content-wise the brief is answered (9/2/4/3 stat band on page 5, ID/Finding/Severity/Status table, per-finding reproduction and remediation, Residual Risk on page 16, nine engineer-days cited), but the rubric is ordered and the empty page 1 alone caps this at level 1. Genericness: apart from the four-number executive band on page 5 and the thin severity rule under the table, this is undifferentiated body text in a default-looking serif/sans pairing — swap the finding text and it would serve as any consultancy's report shell; nothing in the type, colour or page furniture says security assessment.
